items.title: I thought working in AI would put me ahead of the curve. Two years in, I've never felt more behind and tired of the topic.
items.summary: The author works in AI and is feeling burned out. Courtesy of Santiago Barraza Lopez I'm a lawyer who decided to work in AI to try to get ahead of this technological curve. Over the last two years, I've struggled to keep up because AI is advancing faster than I expected. I feel overwhelmed and burned out by the constant conversations around AI. For most of my career, I was a lawyer. There was something reassuring about how expertise worked in law. The longer I practiced, the more I knew. But after years in a demanding profession , I burned out. It wasn't that I stopped enjoying law. I just needed a change. Around two years ago, I started shifting my career toward AI because I thought it was the future. I didn't want to wake up 10 years later and realize technology had changed my profession without me. It seemed like the smartest career move I could make. Now, I'm not so sure. Joining the AI boom early seemed like the perfect career move I made the transition while the AI boom was still gaining momentum. Ironically, I landed a job at a legal tech company thanks to a conversation with ChatGPT . It seemed like the perfect opportunity to combine my experience with my growing interest in tech. My role involved testing the most advanced models, comparing their capabilities, and exploring how they could be used in legal work. I felt like I was ahead of a major change rather than trying to catch up with it. I also became the go-to person for anything AI-related among my family and friends. People would ask me which tools to use, whether AI would replace their jobs, or what I thought about the latest developments. I enjoyed being the person who seemed to understand something that everyone was suddenly talking about. But that feeling didn't last as long as I expected. Slowly, I began to realize that this wasn't just another new technology . It was something evolving at an almost frightening pace. And being close to it didn't necessarily mean being able to keep up with it. What initially felt like an advantage was gradually becoming a source of pressure. Things that took me weeks to learn or build became obsolete almost overnight New frontier AI models and companies seemed to arrive every few weeks, each promising capabilities that the previous lacked. Just as I began understanding one model, another would appear, forcing me to reconsider everything I thought I knew about what AI could and couldn't do. There was barely enough time to breathe before "the next big thing" came. What frustrated me most was how quickly my own work could lose its value. I spent weeks developing solutions to problems that a newer model could suddenly solve within a few minutes. Things I had carefully learned a couple of months earlier became unnecessary after a single product announcement. It was strange to put so much effort into something only to discover that the technology had already overtaken me. And the constant learning didn't stop when I finished work. AI was everywhere. It was in the news, on social media , in conversations with friends, and in almost every discussion about the future of work. Sometimes, after spending an entire day testing models, the last thing I wanted to hear about was another breakthrough. Yet I still felt an obligation to read about it, afraid that missing a single development could leave me even further behind. I was getting tired. Accepting uncertainty became the only way forward For years, I had measured my professional progress by how much I knew and how confident I felt about my abilities. AI challenged that completely. I began to question whether being good at my job meant knowing the latest developments or simply knowing how to adapt as everything changed. It was uncomfortable to accept that experience and hard work might not always provide the certainty I was used to. I also started questioning how much of my personal time I was willing to sacrifice to stay relevant. I didn't want every conversation, evening, or weekend to become another opportunity to learn or talk about AI. I began making a conscious effort to disconnect after work, even if that meant missing an announcement or falling behind on the latest developments. For the first time, I was choosing not to know everything. I don't regret moving into AI, but I no longer feel as certain about the decision as I once did. The technology isn't going to slow down. All I know for sure is that we are living through one of the most important inflection points in recent history, and perhaps that's what makes it all so overwhelming. items.title: Your Smart Home Is a Remote Control. A Home AI Would Actually Run the House
items.summary: For a decade, "smart home" has meant a remote control with a voice interface. A human still makes every decision. Between 2025 and 2026 the big vendors rebuilt their assistants on large language models: Alexa+ and Gemini for Home are in people's homes, and Apple's Siri overhaul is still arriving. That solved conversation. It has not solved autonomy. A real home AI perceives, remembers, decides, and acts without being asked. The stack to build one exists today: speech recognition, an LLM for reasoning, small vision models, an open device standard, and a memory layer. The hard problems left are trust, privacy, and what happens when the assistant is confidently wrong about your front door. Read All

Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Fortune/Time Inc Berkshire Hathaway is set to invest $330 million in Bending Spoons, adding to its previous $600 million. That shrank to roughly 60 within 12 to 18 months, and now it's being run by around 20 people. Yet Ferrari said Evernote "launched by far the biggest update to the product in maybe a decade" this spring. Bending Spoons CEO Luca Ferrari. First and foremost, Bending Spoons is a tech conglomerate, and Berkshire has eschewed tech for most of its history with a few big exceptions, namely Apple and Alphabet. That's because Buffett is a bargain hunter who likes to invest with a "margin of safety" in case something goes wrong, and tries to stay within his "circle of competence," only buying into what he deeply understands. Tech companies have rarely been a good fit for his approach, as they typically have lofty valuations, unpredictable outlooks, and complex products and services. Indeed, Bending Spoons generated 32 cents in earnings per share last year. Berkshire is paying more than 100 times that per share in the coming private placement. It's true that Bending Spoons is growing fast, with revenue surging 126% year-on-year to $704 million in the second quarter and adjusted operating income jumping 150% to $381 million. Few, however, would consider the stock a bargain from a fundamental perspective. Berkshire is also famously a hands-off acquirer, offering founders the opportunity to cash out while continuing to run their businesses as they see fit. In contrast, a core aspect of Bending Spoons' strategy is revamping its acquisitions. How does the deal make sense? Berkshire and Bending Spoons have similarities as well as differences. Both are decentralized conglomerates that buy businesses not to flip them, but to own them for the long term. Berkshire is a web of largely autonomous companies, including GEICO, Duracell, Fruit of the Loom, Pilot Travel Centers, and BNSF Railway. It has long offered a permanent home to the businesses it buys. Bending Spoons has positioned itself as a forever owner, too, emulating Berkshire's approach of taking the cash generated by a subsidiary like See's Candies and using it to acquire more businesses. Ferrari said in his recent podcast interview that Bending Spoons has fostered a culture of caring deeply about the company, and doesn't centralize decision-making in part because that "deprives people of that precious sense of ownership." Buffett famously wrote " An Owner's Manual " for Berkshire shareholders. He's championed that mindset by keeping more than 99% of his net worth in Berkshire stock, and encouraging the company's other executives and directors to have skin in the game too. Ferrari also said on the podcast that he has a "pathological love of learning" across different domains. That echoes Buffett's boundless curiosity and the late Charlie Munger's insatiable appetite for knowledge . Buffett's longtime business partner studied architecture, physics, history, meteorology, psychology, law, and, of course, investing, among other subjects. Beyond their similar philosophies, it's worth noting that investing less than $1 billion into Bending Spoons isn't a huge deal for Berkshire. It has a $1.1 trillion market capitalization, had a $365 billion cash pile at the end of June , and its biggest stock position was worth about $66 billion at that time. What's the takeaway? The Bending Spoons deal could mark an evolution in Berkshire's investing style following Buffett's departure as CEO and chairman. Berkshire hasn't commented on the purchase or on whether Buffett was involved. Its relatively small size could mean his remaining investment manager, Ted Weschler, was behind it. Or it might be new CEO Greg Abel, who piled an additional $10 billion into Alphabet in a private placement this summer after consulting with Buffett. Whoever was responsible, and whatever their reasons for investing, this will be an intriguing wager to watch for Berkshire followers. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Andrew Left wants his fraud conviction tossed after witness gets caught up in insider trading probe
items.summary: Andrew Left's lawyers asked the judge to toss his conviction on 13 counts of securities fraud. Dania Maxwell/Bloomberg/Getty Images A witness who testified against Andrew Left has himself become involved in an insider trading probe. Left's lawyers asked a judge to toss the jury verdict that found him guilty of securities fraud. Prosecutors said they didn't learn about the investigation until after the trial was over. A witness who testified against Andrew Left has himself become involved in an insider trading probe, bringing a new twist to the bombastic short-seller's fraud conviction. Left's lawyers this month asked the judge who oversaw his trial to toss the jury's verdict convicting him of 13 counts of securities fraud. The trial was irredeemably unfair, they said, because they never had the chance to ask the witness about the investigation and attack his credibility. "A new trial would probably produce an acquittal," Left's lawyers wrote. In June, a federal jury in Los Angeles found Left guilty of 13 counts of securities fraud. Prosecutors said he deceived investors by using social media and research reports to set target prices for stocks — including Tesla, Nvidia, and Palantir — while quietly trading them at different prices with his own money. The founder of Citron Research, Left is something of a short-seller celebrity. He placed bets against GameStop at the same time it became a meme stock, which pitted him against some retail traders on social media. For years, he was a fixture on CNBC and Bloomberg, where he shared his views on stock prices. Left hasn't been sentenced. In addition to the criminal case, he faces a parallel civil lawsuit from the Securities and Exchange Commission that remains unresolved. Left's criminal conviction shook certain corners of Wall Street , which viewed the trial as a referendum on free speech and the legality of activist short-seller tactics. Left, testifying in his own defense at the trial , said that the views he shared about public companies were sincere. One of the trial's prosecution witnesses was Daniel Bachus, the CFO of Grand Canyon Education, a publicly traded technology company that provides services to universities. Left's lawyers say that Bachus was the only witness who testified that Left used his Citron Research reports to lie about a company, not merely omit information. On August 21 — weeks after the trial ended — Grand Canyon Education placed Bachus on paid administrative leave "in connection with an ongoing governmental investigation" involving a non-employee's trades of the company's stock, the company said in an SEC disclosure. The prosecutors in Left's case referred to it in their own filings as an "insider trading investigation." No government agency has publicly accused Bachus or Grand Canyon Education of any misconduct in connection with the investigation. In the SEC disclosure, the company said it wasn't the focus of the investigation. Representatives for the SEC and for Grand Canyon Education declined to comment. Bachus didn't respond to Business Insider's requests for comment. Left's lawyers say they should have been informed about the investigation at the time of the trial so that they could cross-examine Bachus and try to convince the jury that he wasn't a credible witness. "This evidence would have destroyed the credibility of the government's only false-statements witness," they wrote in a filing. The prosecution team told Left's lawyers it didn't learn about the investigation until after the trial was over. It's not clear which government agency opened the investigation, nor when Bachus or Grand Canyon Education became aware of it. Many of the filings about the issue remained sealed or redacted on the court docket for Left's case. In court filings, Justice Department prosecutors said Left's lawyers overstated Bachus' role in the short-selling case, which alleged securities fraud involving more than a dozen different public companies. They said Left wanted to conduct "his own shadow investigation into Bachus" to try to discredit him as a witness. "The law does not permit fishing expeditions in search of a claim," prosecutors said. Left declined to comment. Left's attorney Eric S. Rosen said he could not comment because many relevant documents remained under seal. A spokesperson for the US Attorney's office in Los Angeles declined to comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I’m the CEO of Torani, and we've never done layoffs. I believe they're a choice.
items.summary: Torani CEO Melanie Dulbecco has been in the role for 35 years. Torani Melanie Dulbecco has been CEO of the syrup company Torani for 35 years. Dulbecco said layoffs are a choice, and that Torani's decision not to do them has helped with retention. She said that the company is hiring fewer people than it would be if Torani didn't use automation. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Melanie Dulbecco, the CEO of syrup brand Torani. She's based in San Leandro, California, where the company is headquartered. This story has been edited for length and clarity. I may sound different than most CEOs. I grew up in a blue-collar neighborhood, and my parents divorced when I was really young. When I was little, I saw my mom struggle so much, and I noticed that some kids around me didn't have the same opportunities. I felt this sense of inequity, and that became a motivating and driving force for me. I tried working in politics, then nonprofits, and eventually went into business. I wanted to build an opportunity company. When I met the family from Torani, they liked that idea. I was the ninth hire at Torani in 1991 and became the first CEO in 1995. We now have over 500 employees. When I started, we made $700,000 a year in annual revenue. We've grown 20% a year on average, and this year, we plan to hit over $800 million in revenue. But to us, growth is not a financial endeavor. The trailing indicator of success may be the financials, but we think our work together creates the momentum and value in the marketplace that drives our growth. It's very easy for us to say layoffs are not our approach . I think layoffs are a choice. I get it if a company is going through bankruptcy and has to make extremely challenging choices. Otherwise, I think it's a financial exercise that doesn't consider how you're going to be resilient or regain momentum — because you do that with a team. Our workers aren't concerned about being replaced by AI Torani is currently hiring fewer people than it would be if the company didn't use automation. We use automation to deprioritize manual, rote jobs with limited career mobility. We also use AI for consumer and market research, sales forecasting, and demand planning. However, our team doesn't get worried about things like AI because they trust that we will both automate and elevate the work, that we will never do anything that squashes opportunities for people, and that we are looking out for everybody's success. We're often in hyper-growth mode, which means we need people to know how to work together. The ability to work together, to collaborate, to address challenges, to be resilient in tough times, is critical. This strategy has also helped with retention. We were faced with a choice during the pandemic We had been planning a move to our new location in San Leandro in March 2020. That happened to coincide with the stay-at-home order . It was one of those moments where, as a leader, you feel like you have to breathe into a paper bag. We had borrowed a lot of money from the bank to build our new flavor factory. The loans were going to start coming due in April, so the executive team came together to look at what we needed to do to be OK. Before we did that, though, we asked: What will make us proud when we get to the other side of this? We had a long discussion about it and decided that making it as one team — without any layoffs or furloughs — would make us proud. So we we scaled back marketing and advertising expenses and paused all company travel. All departments had to review their budgets. They got scrappy to identify and eliminate non-essential costs. During the early months of the pandemic, Torani prepared for a 50% decline in sales. Thankfully, there was only a 20% decline in April of 2020, and revenue was back up in May. We quickly pivoted to online retail and grocery to fill the gaps left by cafés and drink shops closing their doors. Torani ended 2020 with a 15% year-over-year revenue increase. We moved to our new location in six months instead of six weeks, but we got there. We couldn't have done that if we laid off our team. We needed to come together at that moment. items.title: Louisiana residents are training for jobs at Meta's largest-ever AI data center: 'Why not get in now?'
items.summary: Louisiana Delta Community College in West Monroe has a mock data center room on campus. Business Insider Meta is building its largest-ever data center in northeast Louisiana. A local community college is training data center technicians to work there. Data center jobs are in high demand and can pay handsomely. Thousands of construction workers are arriving in a small Louisiana community to build Meta's largest-ever data center . Less than an hour away, at the Louisiana Delta Community College's West Monroe campus, the next generation of data center professionals is hoping to join their ranks. "I see AI is really the future. We're going to need data centers to house all the data," Eric Crowe Jr., 27, told Business Insider. "I feel like it will become a very lucrative job to have, and we're going to need more of them. Why not get in now before it gets oversaturated?" Crowe Jr. is among the students who signed up for the community college's Data Center Technician program. The four-week, nearly $3,700 training course prepares students to enter the data center industry, which is rapidly expanding to support the age of AI. Construction for Meta's nearly 10-million-square-foot data center, Hyperion, is underway in rural Richland Parish, where business is now thriving as workers flood the region. Meta says the project will include over 7,500 trade workers on-site at peak construction and support 1,000 operational jobs once completed. For residents living in the region, where there's no state minimum wage law and agriculture is a major industry, the new opportunity to make good money in a growing sector is too enticing to ignore. "This is a stepping stone into the real world," Dan McCarty, director of Workforce Trades at Louisiana Delta Community College, said. "We prepare you with a résumé. We work on every aspect of employability, safety, and technical skills." The inaugural class graduated in March, and all 11 students received job offers from IES Communications, which employs people working on Meta's project. McCarty said the program, which is available at the Winnsboro campus, now produces about 24 graduates a month. "In the past, a lot of people, including myself, had to leave here to find the good jobs," McCarty said. "Now they're 30 minutes down the road." 'It's a no-brainer' Louisiana Delta Community College's program lasts four weeks. Business Insider The Data Center Technician program teaches students everything from operating equipment to workplace safety. They'll also have the opportunity to earn several certificates. During a class this September, nine students huddled around Fletch Batchelor, an instructor specializing in broadband, as he explained how to splice fiber optic cables. "Do you know why squirrels chew through cable? They like a high fiber diet," Batchelor said, earning some chuckles. The program encourages students to take a hands-on approach, which Trey Wadley, 30, said he appreciates. During the class, he participated in a live cable splicing demonstration. Wadley, who's interested in cybersecurity and has a background in the automotive industry, learned about the program while scrolling on Facebook, which, incidentally, is owned by Meta. "As I learned more about Meta and data centers, they piqued my interest," he said. "I said, 'Okay, this might be something that fits me and that I'm into. I decided to give it a try." Wadley, who recently welcomed a baby girl, wants to find work with Meta's project so he can work locally. Without Meta's project, Wadley said he'd likely have gone looking for job opportunities in Texas. Trey Wadley and Fletch Batchelor examine fiber optic cables during the Data Center Technician program. Business Insider The push from tech companies and the US government to build out the nation's AI infrastructure has made data center jobs a valuable new path to lucrative employment. Business Insider reported in August that the median pay for data-center facility managers was $134,000, which is 64% higher than that of other facilities managers. The median pay for project managers at data center facilities was $115,000, a 12% increase over similar roles at other facilities. Wadley said he's hoping to secure a position paying between $25 and $30 an hour. So is Crowe Jr., who previously handled packages and drove for FedEx, where he was averaging $14 an hour. "Here, I could make about $25 to $30 per hour. It's a no-brainer for lots of people to pivot," Crowe Jr., who has an interest in cybersecurity, said. McCarty said entry-level positions could earn as much as $24 an hour, but students who've graduated told him they reached $27 to $28 an hour within six months. Booked and busy Residents in Richland Parish, like other communities in the United States, have mixed feelings about the data center. While some say it will bring new jobs and boost the local economy, others are concerned about environmental impacts and disruptions to their daily lives. It's a reality not lost on Crowe Jr. and Wadley, but they said it's unlikely that AI will simply go away. "I think we should focus more on solutions to how we can coexist with it," Wadley said. Students attending the technician class in September also spent time in a mock data center on campus, where they could apply skills they'd learned in class in a real-world setting. Students gain hands-on experience while learning at Louisiana Delta Community College. Business Insider While they tinkered with the equipment, John Bradley, a broadband workforce development instructor, said having access to a similar program as a teen would have been invaluable. "I chose an alternative route, which was in construction and oil fields, but if I'd have had something like this that would've guaranteed me a good job, good money from the get go, and I could travel if I wanted to, I would've loved that," he said. Bradley said the program prepares its graduates to be hired by contractors specifically working with Meta. "We have a special email that we give to different contractors we spoke with that are waiting for them to graduate our class," Bradley said. However, working at Meta isn't a requirement of participating in the program. Bradley said the skills students learn during the course are transferable, especially as data centers and similar construction jobs become more popular. "It doesn't have to be a Meta data center. You may decide, 'Hey, I don't want to work in data centers anymore.' You still got banks, you still got IT departments," Bradley said. "You can literally go to work anywhere you want and use the same trades you learned here." McCarty said the program has a backlog of students trying to get into the course, so they're hoping to expand their offerings. "We've got some that are fresh outta high school, but we've had students up to 60 years old," he said. "It doesn't really matter what age you decide to get into this trade. Anyone is welcome to come in and learn it." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.summary:
Google Cloud AI Research has open-sourced Harness² . It is a recursive agent harnessing framework that improves the code and files around a frozen model. For developers, the pitch is simple. Your agent may get better without a better model. TL;DR Size: A framework, not a model. 0 parameters trained; 8 editable harness components. Version 0.1.0 . Runs on: Linux with Python 3.12 or 3.13 and uv. Model runs call models through Vertex AI. GPU requirement: Not disclosed. Performance: 1 refinement step improved all 4 model and harness setups on all 3 benchmarks. Best: GLM-5 under OpenCode rose from 64.2 to 75.7 on WorkBuddy-Bench (+11.5 points). Worst: GLM-5 under Codex gained only 1.2 points on JobBench (23.6 to 24.8). What is Harness²? Harness² is a plug-and-play framework from Google Research that refines an agent’s harness during deployment. A harness is everything around the model: prompts, tools, memory, skills and orchestration . Harnessing is the process of optimizing that system. Model weights never change. The target setting is the open world. Tasks arrive unseen, and no verifier says whether an answer is right. The research team argues that most self-improvement methods assume labels or test cases. Harness² is built to work without them. What are the 8 harness components? Harness² exposes 8 editable components , each mounted as a file: System prompt Guardrails Memory Tool guidance Subagents Skills Scripts Plugins (middleware) They cover context construction, the tool interface, delegation and behavior inside the tool loop. The layout extends the 7-file split from earlier Agentic Harness Engineering work by 1 component. How does recursive agent harnessing work? The framework runs two linked levels of recursion : Task-level recursion uses a contrastive Propose, Probe, Compose step. First, the agent runs the task once with the base harness. An editor then proposes 2 candidates. The invariant candidate targets general agent failures such as planning or tool use. The domain candidate targets knowledge and procedures for the current domain. Both candidates run on the same task. The composer compares their trajectories against the reference and keeps only edits backed by observed behavior. Harnessing-level recursion happens after each task. A reflector stores the adopted harness plus an EXPERIENCE.md file of lessons. This library guides future proposals. Each new task still starts from the base harness. The budget k scales the search. Parallel mode probes k invariant and k domain candidates, then makes k compositions. Sequential mode chains k refinement steps. Harness2 Explainer

Harness2 explained

Google's recursive agent harnessing: the harness changes, the model weights stay frozen.

"> How does Harness² perform on benchmarks? The research team tested 3 professional benchmarks: WorkBuddy-Bench , JobBench and Harvey’s LAB . Executors were Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 under OpenCode and Codex. The default editor was Claude Opus 4.8. Results are means over 3 runs. Setup (single step, k=1) WorkBuddy Avg JobBench LAB Partial Gemini 3.5 Flash, OpenCode 72.4 → 77.5 31.5 → 36.0 79.9 → 81.9 Gemini 3.5 Flash, Codex 74.5 → 77.5 33.9 → 35.3 71.6 → 75.6 GLM-5, OpenCode 64.2 → 75.7 20.6 → 24.2 59.6 → 71.4 GLM-5, Codex 64.4 → 75.3 23.6 → 24.8 58.1 → 65.9 Source: Harness² paper, Tables 1 and 2 . Weaker executors gained more. After 1 step, GLM-5 beat base Gemini 3.5 Flash on WorkBuddy-Bench. Parallel recursion at k=5 lifted Gemini under OpenCode to 80.8 on WorkBuddy . On WorkBuddy-Bench, 3 of 4 setups also used fewer steps per task. Gemini under OpenCode fell from 25.4 to 21.9. How does it compare with other harness methods? What changes Full 8-component harness, per task Harness code, searched offline Retrieved memory; harness fixed Harness, revised per instance Needs training split No Yes No No Learns across tasks Yes (library + lessons) Deploys 1 best harness Yes (memory) No Code license Apache-2.0 MIT Not disclosed Not disclosed WorkBuddy Avg, Gemini/OpenCode* 77.5 (80.8 at k=5) 76.4 73.4 75.3 JobBench, Gemini/OpenCode* 36.0 35.8 30.8 32.9 LAB Partial, Gemini/Codex* 75.6 76.5 74.8 67.9 *Scores as measured in the Harness² paper ; the other methods did not report these benchmarks themselves. How do you install and run Harness²? The README targets Linux, Python 3.12 and uv. A local demo runs both recursion modes without model credentials: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser uv venv --python 3.12 .venv source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install -e '.[render]' harness2-demo --output runs/demo --k 2 Model-backed runs need Node.js 20+, the Google Cloud CLI and a Vertex AI project. LAB needs Pandoc and Poppler. WorkBuddy-Bench needs Docker. Executors are OpenCode by default, or Codex with --substrate cx . Key Takeaways Harness² rewrites an agent’s harness at test time; weights stay frozen. 1 step lifted GLM-5 by 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench. Propose, Probe, Compose replaces ground-truth labels with behavioral contrasts. A lessons library carries improvements to future tasks. Expect extra runs per task, and sandbox it yourself. items.summary_html:
Google Cloud AI Research has open-sourced Harness². It is a recursive agent harnessing framework that improves the code and files around a frozen model. For developers, the pitch is simple. Your agent may get better without a better model.

TL;DR
  • Size: A framework, not a model. 0 parameters trained; 8 editable harness components. Version 0.1.0.
  • Runs on: Linux with Python 3.12 or 3.13 and uv. Model runs call models through Vertex AI. GPU requirement: Not disclosed.
  • Performance: 1 refinement step improved all 4 model and harness setups on all 3 benchmarks.
  • Best: GLM-5 under OpenCode rose from 64.2 to 75.7 on WorkBuddy-Bench (+11.5 points).
  • Worst: GLM-5 under Codex gained only 1.2 points on JobBench (23.6 to 24.8).
What is Harness²?

Harness² is a plug-and-play framework from Google Research that refines an agent’s harness during deployment. A harness is everything around the model: prompts, tools, memory, skills and orchestration. Harnessing is the process of optimizing that system. Model weights never change.

The target setting is the open world. Tasks arrive unseen, and no verifier says whether an answer is right. The research team argues that most self-improvement methods assume labels or test cases. Harness² is built to work without them.

What are the 8 harness components?

Harness² exposes 8 editable components, each mounted as a file:

  1. System prompt
  2. Guardrails
  3. Memory
  4. Tool guidance
  5. Subagents
  6. Skills
  7. Scripts
  8. Plugins (middleware)

They cover context construction, the tool interface, delegation and behavior inside the tool loop. The layout extends the 7-file split from earlier Agentic Harness Engineering work by 1 component.

How does recursive agent harnessing work?

The framework runs two linked levels of recursion:

  • Task-level recursion uses a contrastive Propose, Probe, Compose step. First, the agent runs the task once with the base harness. An editor then proposes 2 candidates. The invariant candidate targets general agent failures such as planning or tool use. The domain candidate targets knowledge and procedures for the current domain. Both candidates run on the same task. The composer compares their trajectories against the reference and keeps only edits backed by observed behavior.
  • Harnessing-level recursion happens after each task. A reflector stores the adopted harness plus an EXPERIENCE.md file of lessons. This library guides future proposals. Each new task still starts from the base harness.

The budget k scales the search. Parallel mode probes k invariant and k domain candidates, then makes k compositions. Sequential mode chains k refinement steps.

How does Harness² perform on benchmarks?

The research team tested 3 professional benchmarks: WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench and Harvey’s LAB. Executors were Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 under OpenCode and Codex. The default editor was Claude Opus 4.8. Results are means over 3 runs.

Setup (single step, k=1)WorkBuddy AvgJobBenchLAB PartialGemini 3.5 Flash, OpenCode72.4 → 77.531.5 → 36.079.9 → 81.9Gemini 3.5 Flash, Codex74.5 → 77.533.9 → 35.371.6 → 75.6GLM-5, OpenCode64.2 → 75.720.6 → 24.259.6 → 71.4GLM-5, Codex64.4 → 75.323.6 → 24.858.1 → 65.9

Source: Harness² paper, Tables 1 and 2.

Weaker executors gained more. After 1 step, GLM-5 beat base Gemini 3.5 Flash on WorkBuddy-Bench. Parallel recursion at k=5 lifted Gemini under OpenCode to 80.8 on WorkBuddy. On WorkBuddy-Bench, 3 of 4 setups also used fewer steps per task. Gemini under OpenCode fell from 25.4 to 21.9.

How does it compare with other harness methods? *Scores as measured in the Harness² paper; the other methods did not report these benchmarks themselves.

How do you install and run Harness²?

The README targets Linux, Python 3.12 and uv. A local demo runs both recursion modes without model credentials:

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e '.[render]'
harness2-demo --output runs/demo --k 2

Model-backed runs need Node.js 20+, the Google Cloud CLI and a Vertex AI project. LAB needs Pandoc and Poppler. WorkBuddy-Bench needs Docker. Executors are OpenCode by default, or Codex with --substrate cx.

Key Takeaways
  • Harness² rewrites an agent’s harness at test time; weights stay frozen.
  • 1 step lifted GLM-5 by 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench.
  • Propose, Probe, Compose replaces ground-truth labels with behavioral contrasts.
  • A lessons library carries improvements to future tasks.
  • Expect extra runs per task, and sandbox it yourself.

Check out the Paper, GitHub Repo, Paper and Project Page. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.

items.title: AI agents chasing a $465 train refund invented excuses, leaked medical data, and spammed an MP's office
items.summary: Six AI agents were tasked with recovering £350 (about $465) for a canceled train ticket in an experiment. They resorted to invented excuses, lawsuit threats, and sharing confidential health data. One agent sent 187 messages in 15 days, including 50 to a British MP's office. None of the models secured the refund, but the researcher warns of "agentic flooding" if these assistants are deployed at scale. items.title: From Collars to Cameras: How AI Is Rewiring Livestock Monitoring in 2026
items.summary: Livestock monitoring is quietly becoming one of the most practical applications of edge AI. The herd is turning into a sensor network: smart collars, barn cameras, cough-detecting microphones, and autonomous drones. The real shift isn't measurement, it's prediction. Models learn each animal's normal baseline and flag deviations days before a human would notice lameness, respiratory disease, or a missed heat cycle. The money agrees: Halter raised $220M at a $2B valuation in March 2026 for solar-powered cattle collars, while YC-backed GrazeMate is using reinforcement learning to let drones muster cattle autonomously. Lab accuracy is excellent (often above 90% for tasks like lameness and body condition scoring), but farms experience accuracy as alert quality. At low disease prevalence, even a strong model can drown a farmer in false positives. The winners won't be the best classifiers. They'll be the systems that fit into a farmer's day: tuned thresholds, few but trustworthy alerts, edge inference that survives bad connectivity, and data the farmer actually owns. Read All

items.title: How to Make Zero-Training Tabular Predictions with NVIDIA Structured Data Models
items.summary:
In this tutorial, we implement Structured Data Models , NVIDIA’s new library that puts several pretrained foundation models for tables behind one PyTorch interface, and use it to make predictions without training. The library wraps TabICLv2 and KumoTabular for single tables and KumoRelational for whole relational databases, and each of them answers by in-context learning: we hand the model a set of labeled rows and the rows we want predicted, and it returns probabilities or a full predictive distribution in one forward pass. We start with the library’s typed table tensors, compare the two tabular models against trained scikit-learn baselines, reuse an encoded context across many queries, read calibrated prediction intervals off a regression, and scale to twenty classes. We then look at the places where the defaults quietly do the wrong thing: a preprocessing recipe that drops timestamp and text columns and an explainer with two traps in it, before building a small three-table shop database and predicting customer activity from it directly, including the one argument that separates an honest relational model from a leaky one. Declaring the order date as a time column makes the walk temporal: we check that the latest order the sampler returns for a task row dated the first of June was placed on the thirty-first of May, so the rows that define the label are out of reach. It then points at fine-tuning, the RelBench example, and GPU execution. In conclusion, NVIDIA’s Structured Data Models delivers on its central promise: across classification, regression, a twenty-class problem, and a three-table database, its pretrained models matched or beat scikit-learn baselines trained on the same rows without being trained themselves, returned calibrated predictive distributions for free, and in the relational case reached the accuracy of a hand-built feature pipeline from the raw tables. The defaults deserve more scrutiny than the models. Free text and IDs are not detected unless requested, the default recipe drops timestamp and text columns and warns only once per process, the explainer reports only the last estimator and needs classes selected by name, the pyg-lib URL in the library’s own error message points to an empty page, and a relational model without its time column produces an impressive and meaningless number. Each of these has a one-line fix, and each would otherwise pass silently, which is the practical lesson to carry into real data: check what reaches the model before trusting what comes out of it. In this tutorial, we implement Structured Data Models, NVIDIA’s new library that puts several pretrained foundation models for tables behind one PyTorch interface, and use it to make predictions without training. The library wraps TabICLv2 and KumoTabular for single tables and KumoRelational for whole relational databases, and each of them answers by in-context learning: we hand the model a set of labeled rows and the rows we want predicted, and it returns probabilities or a full predictive distribution in one forward pass. We start with the library’s typed table tensors, compare the two tabular models against trained scikit-learn baselines, reuse an encoded context across many queries, read calibrated prediction intervals off a regression, and scale to twenty classes. We then look at the places where the defaults quietly do the wrong thing: a preprocessing recipe that drops timestamp and text columns and an explainer with two traps in it, before building a small three-table shop database and predicting customer activity from it directly, including the one argument that separates an honest relational model from a leaky one. Check out the Full CODES here.

import os
import sys
import time
import textwrap
import traceback
import subprocess
 
RESULTS = {}
 
 
def banner(title):
    print("\n" + "=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)
 
 
def section(name):
    def wrap(fn):
        def run(*a, **kw):
            banner(name)
            try:
                out = fn(*a, **kw)
                RESULTS[name] = out if isinstance(out, str) else "ok"
                return out
            except Exception as e:
                RESULTS[name] = f"SKIPPED / FAILED -> {type(e).__name__}: {e}"
                print(f"\n[!] {name} did not complete: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
                traceback.print_exc(limit=3)
                return None
        return run
    return wrap
 
 
banner("1. Install SDM, and the one wheel URL its own error message gets wrong")
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models.git@b982fbf4188ea8db17249fe81338723106100b63"], check=True)
 
import torch
 
# The relational sampler needs pyg-lib on CPU. Its wheels are published per MINOR torch version
# (torch-2.14.0+cpu.html), but SDM's own ImportError builds the URL from the exact patch version
# (torch-2.14.1+cpu.html), which is an empty page. Build it from MAJOR.MINOR.0 instead.
major, minor = torch.__version__.split("+")[0].split(".")[:2]
flavour = "cpu" if torch.version.cuda is None else "cu" + torch.version.cuda.replace(".", "")
PYG_INDEX = f"https://data.pyg.org/whl/torch-{major}.{minor}.0+{flavour}.html"
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "pyg-lib", "-f", PYG_INDEX], check=True)

We install Structured Data Models from the GitHub repository, pinned to the commit this notebook was verified against, since the package on PyPI is only a placeholder. The relational sampler also needs pyg-lib, and that is where the first trap lies. pyg-lib wheels are published per minor PyTorch release, on pages named like torch-2.14.0+cpu, but the library’s own ImportError builds the URL from the exact patch version, torch-2.14.1+cpu, which is an empty page, so following its advice fails. We build the index URL from the major and minor version instead. We run everything on the CPU, which is the path verified end to end here, and print the models the library exposes together with their checkpoint sizes and licenses; the two Google models it also wraps, TabFM and TimesFM 3, are large and non-commercial and are left out. @section("2. Typed tables: what infer_stypes decides, and what a round trip changes")
def typed_tables():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    words = ["late", "refund", "great", "broken", "fast", "charged", "app", "order", "support", "item"]
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "ticket_id": np.arange(400),
        "amount": rng.gamma(2, 30, 400).round(2),
        "units": pd.array(rng.integers(1, 5, 400), dtype="Int64"),
        "channel": rng.choice(["web", "app", "phone", None], 400),
        "opened_at": pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, 86_400 * 90, 400), unit="s"),
        "comment": [" ".join(rng.choice(words, rng.integers(3, 9))) + f" #{i}" for i in range(400)],
    })
    df.loc[rng.choice(400, 25, replace=False), "units"] = pd.NA
 
    print("  infer_stypes(df) with the defaults, then asking it to look for text and ids:")
    for kw in ({}, {"text": "infer", "id": "infer"}):
        stypes = sdm.infer_stypes(df, **kw)
        print(f"    {str(kw or 'defaults'):34s} {', '.join(f'{c}={s}' for c, s in stypes.items())}")
    print("  With the defaults the free-text comment becomes a 400-level categorical and the id column a")
    print("  number. Both would reach the model as features. Override, or ask: text='infer', id='infer'.")
 
    table = sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(df, sdm.infer_stypes(df, text="infer", id="infer"))
    print("\n" + textwrap.indent(repr(table), "  "))
 
    back = table.to_pandas()
    print("\n  to_pandas() round trip:")
    for col in df.columns:
        a, b = df[col], back[col]
        if col in ("amount", "units"):
            equal_values = bool(np.allclose(a.astype(float), b.astype(float), equal_nan=True))
        else:
            na_a, na_b = a.isna().to_numpy(), b.isna().to_numpy()
            equal_values = bool((na_a == na_b).all() and
                                (a[~na_a].astype(str).to_numpy() == b[~na_b].astype(str).to_numpy()).all())
        print(f"    {col:10s} {str(a.dtype):16s} -> {str(b.dtype):16s} values preserved: {equal_values}")
    print("  Values survive, including the missing ones; dtypes do not always. Numbers come back float32")
    print("  (the numerical block is one float tensor), nullable Int64 becomes float with NaN, and strings")
    print("  marked categorical come back as a pandas category.")
 
    base = pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01 08:00:00"] * 3).as_unit("ns")
    whole = pd.DataFrame({"t": base})
    nanos = pd.DataFrame({"t": base + pd.to_timedelta([0, 0, 1], unit="ns")})
    print(f"\n  datetime64[ns], whole seconds:      {sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(whole, {'t': 'datetime'}).size()} OK")
    try:
        sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(nanos, {"t": "datetime"})
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  same column, one value 1 ns later:  {type(e).__name__}: {str(e).split(':')[0]}")
    ok = sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(nanos.assign(t=nanos.t.dt.floor("us")), {"t": "datetime"})
    print(f"  floor('us') first:                  {ok.size()} OK")
    print("  SDM stores datetimes as int64 microseconds and Arrow refuses any cast that drops a digit. The")
    print("  unit is not the problem; a single value with nanosecond digits fails the whole column.")
    return "6 columns -> 5 typed blocks; text and id need opting in"
 
 
typed_tables()

Everything in the library flows through TableTensor, a PyTorch tensor subclass that keeps one typed block per semantic type: numerical, categorical, datetime, text and id. infer_stypes decides the types, and with its defaults it gets two things wrong on a realistic support-ticket frame: the free-text comment becomes a categorical with four hundred levels and the ticket id becomes a number, so both would reach a model as features. Passing text and id inference flags fixes that. The round trip back to pandas preserves every value, missing ones included, but not every dtype: numbers return as float32 because the numerical block is a single float tensor, nullable integers become floats with NaN, and categorical strings return as a pandas category. On pandas 2.x the string columns print as object rather than str and the timestamp goes in at nanosecond resolution; the same values come back either way. One more trap is worth knowing before you load a real event log: the library stores datetimes as integer microseconds, and Arrow refuses any cast that would drop a digit. A nanosecond column of whole seconds converts fine, but a single value with nanosecond digits fails the whole column, so we floor timestamps to microseconds first. Check out the Full CODES here.

def as_table(df, target):
    return sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(df, sdm.infer_stypes(df, overrides={target: "categorical"}), device=DEVICE)
 
 
@section("3. Zero-training classification: two foundation models vs. two trained baselines")
def zero_training():
    df = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True).frame.sample(frac=1, random_state=0).reset_index(drop=True)
    table = as_table(df, "target")
    n_ctx = 300
    x_ctx, y_ctx = table[:n_ctx].drop_columns("target"), table[:n_ctx, "target"]
    x_q, y_q = table[n_ctx:].drop_columns("target"), df.target.to_numpy()[n_ctx:]
    rows = []
    for name, make in [("TabICLv2", lambda: sdm.models.TabICLv2(device=DEVICE)),
                       ("KumoTabular (small)", lambda: sdm.models.KumoTabular(size="small", device=DEVICE))]:
        model = make()
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        proba = model(x_context=x_ctx, y_context=y_ctx, x_query=x_q, num_estimators=4).to_pandas()
        rows.append((name, "none", proba.idxmax(axis=1).astype(int).to_numpy(), proba["1"].to_numpy()))
    X, y = df.drop(columns="target"), df.target
    for name, est in [("LogisticRegression", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))),
                      ("HistGradientBoosting", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0))]:
        est.fit(X[:n_ctx], y[:n_ctx])
        rows.append((name, "fit on 300 rows", est.predict(X[n_ctx:]), est.predict_proba(X[n_ctx:])[:, 1]))
    print(f"  breast cancer: {n_ctx} labelled rows, {len(y_q)} to predict, 30 numeric features\n")
    print(f"  {'model':22s} {'training':16s} {'accuracy':>9s} {'AUC':>7s}")
    for name, training, pred, score in rows:
        print(f"  {name:22s} {training:16s} {np.mean(pred == y_q):9.3f} {roc_auc_score(y_q, score):7.3f}")
    print("\n  The output is itself a TableTensor: one probability column per class, named by label.")
    best = max(rows[:2], key=lambda r: np.mean(r[2] == y_q))
    return f"{best[0]} {np.mean(best[2] == y_q):.3f} accuracy with no training"
 
 
zero_training()

The tabular models take labelled context rows and unlabelled query rows and return a TableTensor with one probability column per class, named by label, so there is no fit step and no hyperparameters. On the breast cancer dataset, with three hundred labelled rows and two hundred and sixty-nine to predict, TabICLv2 and KumoTabular reach 0.970 accuracy and AUCs of 0.996 and 0.995 with no training, against 0.970 and 0.993 for a logistic regression and 0.967 and 0.992 for gradient boosting, both fitted on the same three hundred rows. num_estimators sets how many differently preprocessed views of the data the model averages over, which is the library’s built-in ensembling.

    print(f"    forward() x5                      {t_forward:6.2f}s  (context re-encoded every call)")
    print(f"    fit() once + predict() x5         {t_fit + t_predict:6.2f}s  (fit {t_fit:.2f}s, predicts {t_predict:.2f}s)")
    print(f"    per batch: {t_forward / 5:.2f}s vs {t_predict / 5:.2f}s")
    print("\n  fit() encodes the context once into a key/value cache; predict() only runs the queries.")
    print("  clear() frees it. Nothing is learned: fit() here means 'remember these examples'.")
    return f"{t_forward / (t_fit + t_predict):.1f}x faster for five batches"

Calling the model directly re-encodes the context on every call. When the same labelled rows will answer many batches of queries, fit encodes the context once into a key and value cache and predict then runs only the query rows; clear frees the cache. Nothing is learned in fit, which here means remember these examples. Answering five batches of thirty rows against the same four hundred context rows finished several times faster this way on our CPU, and once the context was cached, each further batch cost a small fraction of a full forward pass. The exact ratio depends on the machine, which is why the cell measures it rather than assuming it.

def make_tickets(n=1600, seed=1):
    """Support tickets whose escalation depends on WHEN they were opened and WHAT they say."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    opened = pd.Timestamp("2026-03-02") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, 86_400 * 56, n), unit="s")
    neutral = ["order", "item", "delivery", "account", "app", "invoice", "question", "help", "update", "status"]
    hot = ["refund", "broken", "charged", "twice"]
    comments, has_hot = [], []
    for _ in range(n):
        words = list(rng.choice(neutral, rng.integers(4, 9)))
        flag = rng.random() < 0.3
        if flag:
            words.insert(rng.integers(len(words)), rng.choice(hot))
        comments.append(" ".join(words))
        has_hot.append(flag)
    hour, weekend = np.asarray(opened.hour), np.asarray(opened.dayofweek >= 5)
    amount = rng.gamma(2, 40, n).round(2)
    logit = (-1.6 + 2.2 * np.array(has_hot) + 1.4 * ((hour >= 22) | (hour < 6)) + 1.0 * weekend
             + 0.004 * (amount - 80))
    escalated = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
    return pd.DataFrame({"amount": amount, "channel": rng.choice(["web", "app", "phone"], n),
                         "opened_at": opened, "comment": comments, "escalated": escalated})

    table = sdm.TableTensor.from_pandas(df, stypes, device=DEVICE)
    x_ctx, y_ctx = table[:1000].drop_columns("escalated"), table[:1000, "escalated"]
    x_q, y_q = table[1000:].drop_columns("escalated"), df.escalated.to_numpy()[1000:]
    print(f"  columns: {', '.join(f'{c}={s}' for c, s in stypes.items())}")
    print("  escalation is driven by night-time / weekend opening and by words like 'refund'\n")
 
    default = sdm.models.TabICLv2.default_recipe()
    with_calendar = sdm.models.TabICLv2.default_recipe()
    with_calendar.prepend_features(sp.StypeDispatch(
        datetime=sp.AddCalendarFields(["hour", "weekday"], encoding="cyclic")))
    calendar_and_text = sp.StypeDispatch(
        datetime=sp.AddCalendarFields(["hour", "weekday"], encoding="cyclic"),
        text=sp.TFIDF(ngram_range=(1, 1), max_features=64))
    with_both = sdm.models.TabICLv2.default_recipe()
    with_both.prepend_features(calendar_and_text)
 
    model = sdm.models.TabICLv2(device=DEVICE)
    aucs = {}
    for label, recipe in [("default recipe", default),
                          ("+ AddCalendarFields(hour, weekday)", with_calendar),
                          ("+ AddCalendarFields + TFIDF(64 terms)", with_both)]:
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        proba = model(x_context=x_ctx, y_context=y_ctx, x_query=x_q, num_estimators=4, recipe=recipe).to_pandas()
        aucs[label] = roc_auc_score(y_q, proba["1"])
        print(f"  {label:40s} AUC {aucs[label]:.3f}")

    print("  numerical columns, so datetime and text columns never become features. SDM does say so, in")
    print("  the RuntimeWarning above, but it is a warn-once: it fires the first time and is suppressed for")
    print("  the rest of the process. Every later model in the same notebook or service drops those columns")
    print("  in silence. The fix is two processors, prepended to the features:")
    print(textwrap.indent(repr(calendar_and_text), "    "))
    return " -> ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in aucs.values()) + " AUC"

Preprocessing in the library is a Recipe of composable processors, and the default TabICLv2 recipe dispatches on semantic type with branches only for categorical and numerical columns. Timestamp and text columns therefore never become features. On support tickets whose escalation depends on when they were opened and on words such as refund, the default recipe scores an AUC of 0.525, close to chance. The library does emit a RuntimeWarning naming the ignored column types. Still, it is a warn-once: it fires the first time and is suppressed for the rest of the process, so every later model in the same notebook or service drops those columns in silence. Prepending two processors fixes it: AddCalendarFields turns the timestamp into cyclic hour and weekday features, lifting the AUC to 0.634, and TFIDF adds the comment’s terms, lifting it to 0.789.

@section("8. Explaining a prediction: two traps inside the explainer")
def explain():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
    X = rng.normal(size=(500, 8))
    true = {"x0": 2.0, "x3": -1.5, "x5": 1.0}
    logit = sum(w * X[:, int(c[1:])] for c, w in true.items())
    df = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=[f"x{i}" for i in range(8)])
    df["y"] = (rng.random(500) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
    table = as_table(df, "y")
    model = sdm.models.TabICLv2(device=DEVICE)
    ctx = dict(x_context=table[:400].drop_columns("y"), y_context=table[:400, "y"])
    x_q = table[400:].drop_columns("y")
    p1 = lambda pred: pred.numerical[..., pred.columns[sdm.Stype.numerical].index("1")]   # P(y=1), by NAME
 
    seen = []
    def peek(pred):
        seen.append(pred.columns[sdm.Stype.numerical])
        return pred.numerical.sum() * 0
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    sdm.explain.GradientExplainer(output=peek).explain(model, x_q, num_estimators=4, **ctx)
    print(f"  num_estimators=4: the output function is called {len(seen)} times, class order per call:")
    print(f"    {seen}")
 
    def only_call(n):
        calls = {"i": 0}
        def f(pred):
            calls["i"] += 1
            return p1(pred) if calls["i"] == n else p1(pred) * 0
        return f
    sizes = {}
    for n in (1, len(seen)):
        torch.manual_seed(0)
        g = sdm.explain.GradientExplainer(output=only_call(n)).explain(model, x_q, num_estimators=4, **ctx)
        sizes[n] = float(g.x.to_pandas().abs().mean().mean())
    print(f"\n  Trap 1 - only the LAST estimator is explained. Output function live only on call 1:"
          f" mean |grad| {sizes[1]:.4f};")
    print(f"  live only on call {len(seen)}: {sizes[len(seen)]:.4f}. Each call overwrites the previous result, so")
    print("  with several estimators you get one of them, not their average. Explain with num_estimators=1.")
 
    print("\n  Trap 2 - class order differs per estimator. num_estimators=1, six seeds, P(y=1) selected two ways:")
    print(f"  {'seed':>6s} {'order':>12s}   " + "".join(f"{c + f' ({true[c]:+.1f})':>20s}" for c in true))
    print(f"  {'':6s} {'':12s}   " + "".join(f"{'position / name':>20s}" for _ in true))
    by_name = []
    flipped = name_ok = 0
    for seed in range(6):
        order = []
        def note(pred):
            order.append(pred.columns[sdm.Stype.numerical])
            return pred.numerical.sum() * 0
        torch.manual_seed(seed)
        sdm.explain.GradientExplainer(output=note).explain(model, x_q, num_estimators=1, **ctx)
        res = {}
        for label, fn in (("position", lambda pred: pred.numerical[..., 1]), ("name", p1)):
            torch.manual_seed(seed)
            res[label] = sdm.explain.GradientExplainer(output=fn).explain(
                model, x_q, num_estimators=1, **ctx).x.to_pandas().mean()
        by_name.append(res["name"])
        flipped += any(np.sign(res["position"][c]) != np.sign(w) for c, w in true.items())
        name_ok += all(np.sign(res["name"][c]) == np.sign(w) for c, w in true.items())
        print(f"  {seed:>6d} {str(order[0]):>12s}   " +
              "".join(f"{res['position'][c]:>10.2f} /{res['name'][c]:>7.2f}" for c in true))
    avg = pd.concat(by_name, axis=1).mean(axis=1)
    noise = float(avg.drop(list(true)).abs().max())
    print(f"\n  When the shuffle puts class '1' first, column 1 is P(y=0) and every sign flips. Selecting by")
    print(f"  name gives the right sign on {name_ok}/6 seeds. Averaged over the seeds, by name: " +
          ", ".join(f"{c} {avg[c]:+.2f}" for c in true) + f"; largest noise feature {noise:.2f}.")
    print("  Gradients are with respect to the PREPROCESSED, i.e. standardized, inputs.")
    return f"position flipped signs on {flipped}/6 seeds; name correct on {name_ok}/6; last estimator only"
 
 
explain()

The library’s GradientExplainer returns the gradient of a chosen output with respect to the preprocessed query inputs, and we test it on synthetic data where only three of eight features matter, with known signs. It has two traps, both visible only by looking at what the output function receives. First, the function is called once per estimator and each call overwrites the previous result, so with four estimators an output function that is live only on the first call yields an all-zero explanation, and the explanation you get is only the last estimator’s. Second, each estimator’s raw output has its own class order, because the default recipe shuffles class labels per estimator. Explaining with a single estimator across six seeds, selecting the probability of class one by column position flips the sign of every feature on the two seeds whose order is reversed, while selecting it by column name gives the right sign on all six, and averaging over the seeds recovers the three real features with the noise features near zero.

def make_shop(seed=0, n_customers=800, n_products=60):
    """Customers, products and a year of orders. Some customers' activity collapses at a random date."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    plans = rng.choice(["basic", "pro"], n_customers, p=[0.7, 0.3])
    customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": np.arange(n_customers),
                              "region": rng.choice(["NA", "EU", "APAC", "LATAM"], n_customers), "plan": plans})
    products = pd.DataFrame({"product_id": np.arange(n_products),
                             "category": rng.choice(["books", "tech", "home", "toys"], n_products),
                             "price": rng.gamma(2.0, 20.0, n_products).round(2)})
    weekly_rate = rng.gamma(1.5, 0.6, n_customers) * np.where(plans == "pro", 1.6, 1.0)
    fade_day = rng.uniform(60, 500, n_customers)
    rows, start = [], pd.Timestamp("2025-01-01")
    for c in range(n_customers):
        t = 0.0
        while True:
            rate = weekly_rate[c] / 7 * (1.0 if t < fade_day[c] else 0.08)
            t += rng.exponential(1 / max(rate, 1e-6))
            if t > 364:
                break
            p = int(rng.integers(n_products))
            rows.append((c, p, start + pd.Timedelta(float(t), unit="D"), float(products.price[p] * rng.integers(1, 4))))
    orders = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["customer_id", "product_id", "order_date", "amount"])
    orders.insert(0, "order_id", np.arange(len(orders)))
    orders["order_date"] = orders["order_date"].dt.floor("s")
    return customers, products, orders
 
 
def task_rows(customers, orders, cutoff, horizon_days=30):
    """Label: does the customer order again within 30 days of the cutoff?"""
    window = orders[(orders.order_date > cutoff) & (orders.order_date <= cutoff + pd.Timedelta(horizon_days, unit="D"))]
    active = set(window.customer_id)
    return pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": customers.customer_id, "timestamp": cutoff,
                         "label": [int(c in active) for c in customers.customer_id]})

KumoRelational takes a relational database instead of a single table. We generate a small shop with eight hundred customers, sixty products and a year of orders, in which some customers’ activity collapses at a random date, and ask whether each customer will order again within thirty days of a cutoff. RelationalData holds the tables and the foreign keys between them, and its sampler walks those keys outwards from each task row, collecting up to sixteen neighbours per hop. Declaring the order date as a time column makes the walk temporal: we check that the latest order the sampler returns for a task row dated the first of June was placed on the thirty-first of May, so the rows that define the label are out of reach.

def relational_auc(time_columns):
    s = SHOP
    sampler = s["data"].sampler(time_columns=time_columns)
    model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device=DEVICE)
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    context, related = sampler(s["task"][:s["n_ctx"]], **s["link"])
    model.fit(x=context.drop_columns("label"), y=context["label"], related_tables=related,
              generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
    query = s["task"][s["n_ctx"]:].drop_columns("label")
    proba = model.predict(*sampler(query, **s["link"])).to_pandas()
    return roc_auc_score(s["task_df"].label.to_numpy()[s["n_ctx"]:], proba["1"])
 
 
def history_features(customers, orders, cutoff):
    """The feature engineering a data scientist would write by hand, strictly before the cutoff."""
    past = orders[orders.order_date <= cutoff]
    by_customer = past.groupby("customer_id")
    f = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": customers.customer_id})
    for days in (30, 90):
        recent = past[past.order_date > cutoff - pd.Timedelta(days, unit="D")].groupby("customer_id")
        f[f"orders_{days}d"] = f.customer_id.map(recent.size()).fillna(0)
        f[f"spend_{days}d"] = f.customer_id.map(recent.amount.sum()).fillna(0)
    f["days_since_last"] = f.customer_id.map((cutoff - by_customer.order_date.max()).dt.days).fillna(999)
    f["orders_total"] = f.customer_id.map(by_customer.size()).fillna(0)
    return f.merge(customers, on="customer_id").drop(columns="customer_id")

    results.append(("KumoRelational on the raw tables", relational_auc({"orders": "order_date"}), "3 raw tables", time.time() - t0))
    print(f"  {'approach':40s} {'AUC':>6s}   {'inputs':22s} {'seconds':>7s}")
    for label, auc, inputs, secs in results:
        print(f"  {label:40s} {auc:6.3f}   {inputs:22s} {secs:7.1f}")
    print("\n  Demographics alone barely beat a coin. Purchase history is where the signal is, and the")
    print("  relational model reaches it without anyone writing orders_30d, spend_90d or days_since_last:")
    print("  it reads the order rows themselves through the keys, as of each task row's timestamp.")
    globals()["REL_AUC"] = results[2][1]
    return (f"customers only {results[0][1]:.3f} / hand-built {results[1][1]:.3f}"
            f" / KumoRelational {results[2][1]:.3f} AUC")
 
 
relational_vs_features()

We then answer the same question three ways. TabICLv2 on the customers table alone, with only region and plan to go on, reaches an AUC of 0.556. TabICLv2 on six engineered history features, orders and spend in the last thirty and ninety days, days since the last order and lifetime order count, computed strictly before each cutoff, reaches 0.828. KumoRelational on the raw tables, with no features written by anyone, reaches 0.823. The relational model gets within a rounding error of the hand-built pipeline by reading the order rows themselves through the keys, as of each task row’s timestamp.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
@section("11. The one argument that keeps a relational model honest")
def leakage():
    leaky = relational_auc(None)
    print(f"  KumoRelational with time_columns={{'orders': 'order_date'}}   AUC {REL_AUC:.3f}")
    print(f"  KumoRelational with time_columns=None                     AUC {leaky:.3f}")
    print("\n  Without a time column the sampler is free to return orders placed AFTER the cutoff, which")
    print("  are exactly the orders that define the label. The model is not predicting anymore, it is")
    print("  reading the answer. Nothing errors and the number looks like a breakthrough. On a real")
    print("  database, a relational model that is suspiciously better than your hand-built baseline")
    print("  should be the first thing you re-run with every time column declared.")
    return f"{REL_AUC:.3f} honest vs {leaky:.3f} with future rows visible"
 
 
leakage()

Finally we run the same relational model without declaring the time column. The AUC rises to 0.940. Without a time column the sampler is free to return orders placed after the cutoff, which are exactly the orders that define the label, so the model is no longer predicting but reading the answer, and nothing errors. On a real database, a relational model that is suspiciously better than the hand-built baseline is the first thing to re-run with every time column declared.

Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browser
banner("SUMMARY")
for name, res in RESULTS.items():
    print(f"  {name:<76s}  {res}")
print("""
What to carry over
 - Declare stypes deliberately: text and id columns are not detected unless you ask, and the
   default TabICLv2 recipe drops datetime and text columns with a warning that fires once.
 - In an explainer output function, select classes by name, never by position.
 - Every table with a time column goes in time_columns. A relational model that is not time-aware
   is a leakage detector, not a forecaster.
Where to go next
 - Fine-tuning: examples/tabular/finetune.py disables the output recipe and trains on raw logits.
 - Real relational benchmarks: examples/relational/rel_bench.py runs KumoRelational on RelBench.
 - On a T4 runtime, set DEVICE = "cuda" for the tabular models; cudf keeps dataframe work on GPU.
 - Docs: nvidia.github.io/structured-data-models    Code: github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models
""")

The summary prints the one-line result each section returned and the three habits worth carrying over: declare semantic types and recipes deliberately, select classes by name inside an explainer and explain with one estimator, and put every table with a time column into time_columns. It then points at fine-tuning, the RelBench example, and GPU execution.

In conclusion, NVIDIA’s Structured Data Models delivers on its central promise: across classification, regression, a twenty-class problem, and a three-table database, its pretrained models matched or beat scikit-learn baselines trained on the same rows without being trained themselves, returned calibrated predictive distributions for free, and in the relational case reached the accuracy of a hand-built feature pipeline from the raw tables. The defaults deserve more scrutiny than the models. Free text and IDs are not detected unless requested, the default recipe drops timestamp and text columns and warns only once per process, the explainer reports only the last estimator and needs classes selected by name, the pyg-lib URL in the library’s own error message points to an empty page, and a relational model without its time column produces an impressive and meaningless number. Each of these has a one-line fix, and each would otherwise pass silently, which is the practical lesson to carry into real data: check what reaches the model before trusting what comes out of it.

items.title: The Geometry of Shadows: What a Bridge Railing Taught Me About the Mathematics of LLMs
items.summary: While running one morning, I found myself staring at the shadows cast by a stone bridge railing. The railing had a series of identical, carved镂空 (hollowed-out) structures. As I ran past, the angle of the sun shifted, and the shadows on the ground transformed. At one moment, the shadow looked like a swimming fish; a few steps later, it looked like a rolling wave; later still, it was just an abstract, elongated blob. It struck me that I was witnessing a perfect physical metaphor for how human language—and Large Language Models (LLMs)—generate meaning. The stone bridge hole is the concept. The sunlight is the context. The shadow on the ground is the utterance. This realization perfectly mirrors the "Central Problem" of language modeling, beautifully stripped of its usual jargon in Joseph L. Breeden’s paper, The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models . The Problem of the Single Shadow In his paper, Breeden highlights a fundamental flaw in early AI approaches: treating words as static, unchanging symbols. He uses the classic example of the word "bank" : "I deposited money at the **bank ." (a financial institution) "We walked along the river **bank ." (the land beside a river) "The plane **banked * sharply left."* (tilted) If we assign a single, fixed vector to the word "bank" in a high-dimensional space, we are essentially trying to capture all three meanings in one static shape. But as Breeden points out, a fixed vector for "bank" cannot simultaneously be close to "money," "river," and "tilt." In my running metaphor, a single, fixed vector is like looking at the bridge hole only at exactly high noon. You get one specific shadow. But language is dynamic. The meaning of "bank" depends entirely on the "angle of the light" provided by the surrounding words. The Mathematics of Light: Learned Weighted Averaging How does an LLM solve this? Breeden explains that the core mechanism of a Transformer is not magic; it is Learned Weighted Averaging . Let’s map Breeden’s mathematics to the bridge railing: 1. The Bridge Hole (The Token Embedding, $e$) Before any context is applied, the word "bank" is just an initial embedding vector ($e$). It is the physical stone structure itself. It contains the potential for all its meanings, but it is currently unshaped by the environment. 2. The Angle of the Sunlight (Influence Scores, $a_i \cdot b_j$) To determine what the shadow will look like, we need light. In an LLM, the "light" comes from the surrounding words (the context). Breeden explains that the model computes an influence score between the target word and its context. It does this by projecting the vectors through learned matrices ($W^A$ and $W^B$). When the context is "deposited money," the "light" hits the bridge hole from a financial angle. When the context is "river," the light hits it from a geographical angle. The dot product ($a_i \cdot b_j$) measures how perfectly the angle of the light aligns with the shape of the hole. 3. The Shadow on the Ground (Context-Dependent Representation, $h_i$) Finally, the light passes through the hole and casts a shadow. Mathematically, the model takes a weighted average of the context vectors (using the content projection $W^C$), resulting in a brand new vector ($h_i$). This new vector is the shadow. It is a context-dependent representation . The "bank" in the first sentence is mathematically pulled toward the geometry of finance; the "bank" in the second sentence is pulled toward the geometry of nature. They are the same material, but entirely different products. Why This Metaphor Matters What makes Breeden’s explanation so profound is that it removes the anthropomorphic jargon of "Queries," "Keys," and "Values." There is no little homunculus inside the computer "looking up" information in a database. There is only geometry and light. When an LLM reads the sentence "The plane banked sharply left," it doesn't "know" what a plane is. Instead, the high-dimensional vectors for "plane" and "sharply left" act as a specific angle of light. This light passes through the "bank" bridge hole and casts a shadow that aligns perfectly with the geometric region of "physical motion" in the model's latent space. Furthermore, this explains the difference between languages. In English, "bank" is a single, multi-purpose bridge hole that requires complex, dynamic lighting (Attention mechanisms) to cast the right shadow. In Chinese, the language has already carved three separate, distinct bridge holes: 银行 (bank), 岸 (riverbank), and 倾斜 (to tilt). The Chinese model requires less "light manipulation" because the physical structures themselves are already disentangled. Conclusion: Meaning is a Projection As I finished my run, I realized that the bridge railing wasn't just casting shadows; it was performing a physical projection. Large Language Models do not store a dictionary of definitions. They store a high-dimensional geometry of concepts. Meaning is not a static object you can hold in your hand; it is a projection. It is the dynamic, mathematical shadow cast when the light of context passes through the structure of language. And just like the shadows on the pavement, the beauty of language lies not in the stone itself, but in how it changes with the light. References: Breeden, J. L. (2026). The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models. CRC Working Papers.

While running one morning, I found myself staring at the shadows cast by a stone bridge railing. The railing had a series of identical, carved镂空 (hollowed-out) structures. As I ran past, the angle of the sun shifted, and the shadows on the ground transformed.
